title: Never Stand on Wall Top Plates Without Fall Protection
summary: A 22-year-old framer died after falling about 24 feet from the top plate of a second-story wall. He had no fall protection or training. The foreman had told him to get down but walked away. Protect every worker at 6 feet or more.
talking_points: The worker climbed a stepladder to reach the top plate of an exterior second-story wall and stepped onto it. He had no fall protection. A short time later he lost his balance coming down and fell about 24 feet to frozen ground.
The foreman saw him on the plate and told him to get down and use the stepladder, but then walked away. Telling a worker to get down is not enough. Fix the setup so the work can be done safely.
Fall protection is required for exposure of 6 feet or more in residential framing. Use a guardrail system, a safety net, or a personal fall arrest system.
Install guardrails early on new construction: along floor and roof edges, across door and window openings, and around open stairwells. Keep them in place and move them as needed.
Training is required on fall protection, ladders, and scaffolds. Ladder training covers choosing the right ladder for the job, including its type, length, and duty rating.
Employers need a safety program that covers hazard recognition, fall protection, ladders, floor openings, nail guns, and PPE, and they must enforce it.
site_hazards_to_check: Workers walking or standing on wall top plates
Open edges, open stairwells, and openings in unfinished floors
Stepladders set up next to open walls where a fall to the outside is possible
Hard or frozen ground below an open edge
No fall protection or ladder training for new workers
discussion_questions: How will each person reach high framing work without standing on a top plate?
Where is fall protection set up for second-floor and roof-level work?
Who has had fall protection and ladder training for this job?
